source.value: Carrots are one of the tastiest vegetables to pull fresh from the garden, with a sweetness and earthy flavour that is hard to match from shop-bought roots. They are also one of the more awkward crops to establish well: germination can be slow, seedlings are vulnerable to slugs, and the roots need deep, fine, stone-free soil if they are to grow straight and tender. Once growing, however, carrots are very rewarding, especially if sown in short successions so that roots can be lifted from early summer into autumn. Good moisture, careful thinning, and protection from carrot fly make a big difference. In lighter soils or compost-filled no-dig beds they can be excellent, but fresh manure, compacted ground, stones, drought and rough handling all tend to produce forked, tough or damaged roots.

Recommended varieties
SHORT-ROOTED
Early Nantes 2

A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Autumn King

A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Chantenay Red Cored

A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

Key risks
Carrot Fly

Tell-tale signs on carrots are reddish leaves which wilt in sunny weather and later turn yellow.

Fanging

Fanging is usually caused by adding manure or compost to the soil shortly before seed sowing.

Small Roots

Aphids and virus will stunt growth and reduce yield, but even in the absence of pests and diseases many gardeners produce disappointingly small carrots.

Splitting

Much more serious than fanging of carrots, because the roots will not store.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
14

Growing guide · Carrot
Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow thinly

Sow direct, very thinly, in shallow drills.

2 Cover lightly

Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.

3 Thin later

Thin seedlings to the final spacing in Quick facts.

Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist.

Looking after the crop
Thin only as needed in evenings or damp weather; water dry soil first. Firm afterwards and clear thinnings: bruised roots attract carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.
Trim leaves about 1/2 in. above the crown. Store sound roots separately in sand, cool, ventilated and just above freezing; they may keep until March.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Carrot Fly	Tunnelled roots.	Use fine mesh; remove thinnings; avoid bruising.
Fanging	Forked roots	Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.
Small Roots	Small roots; weak growth.	Improve soil; use organic feed if growth is poor.
Splitting	Split roots.	Water evenly; mulch in drought; use split roots now.
Sclerotinia Rot	White mould; rotting roots.	Remove diseased roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Carrot-Willow Aphid	Distorted, stunted leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Black Rot	Black lesions on stored roots.	Remove rotten roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Motley Dwarf Virus	Yellow mottling; red outer leaves.	No cure; remove affected plants. Monitor aphids.
Green Top	Green exposed crowns.	Earth up to cover exposed root tops.
Violet Root Rot	Purple felt-like growth on roots.	Destroy affected roots; never store them; rotate.
Final tips

Avoid fresh manure and disturbance around established roots.

Work from one end of the row when harvesting.

Inspect stored roots and remove any that rot.

Root Crops
Celeriac.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base. Its earthy celery flavour suits soups, stews, salads and winter dishes; lifted roots keep into spring if stored cool. It needs less blanching and earthing-up work than celery, but still needs a full season, a good start under cover and rich, moisture-retentive soil. Shallow, fibrous roots suffer in dry ground: water steadily in dry weather. Heavy, well-composted soil suits it well; varieties are broadly similar.

Recommended varieties
Prinz

A dependable celeriac for rounded roots and useful kitchen quality. A strong first choice for the main crop.

Monarch

A modern celeriac with pale flesh and comparatively smooth roots. A useful addition for easier preparation in the kitchen.

Asterix F1

An early hybrid producing large, round roots for autumn harvesting and storage. Useful bolting resistance helps support a dependable crop.

Giant Prague

A long-established celeriac with large roots. Retain as a heritage alternative where seed cost and traditional varieties matter.

Key risks
SLUGS

Slugs can damage seedlings and later chew holes in swollen roots.

CARROT FLY

Brown lines or tunnels across the lower part of the root may be caused by carrot root fly maggots.

FROST

Celeriac is hardy, but exposed roots and frozen ground can make winter harvesting difficult.

Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)

Celery leaf miner makes pale blotches that turn brown and papery.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
16

Growing guide · Celeriac
Keep growth steady from the start.

Cold or drought checks can reduce the crop and encourage bolting.

Keep the crown at soil level.

Celeriac needs no celery-style earthing up or blanching.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of well-rotted compost. Improved heavier ground often suits shallow-rooted celeriac.
Mulch to conserve moisture; add an appropriate organic feed only if the soil lacks fertility.
Sowing & planting
1 Surface sow

Sow March–April under cover. Moist compost; barely cover seed.

2 Grow on

Prick out into modules. Avoid cold and drought; harden off before planting.

3 Keep the crown clear

Plant after late frosts, stem-base at soil level. Firm and water; do not earth up.

Looking after the crop
Weed until leaves cover the ground. Water in dry weather and maintain a compost mulch: shallow roots dry quickly, checking the swollen stem-base’s growth.
Keep soil and mulch off crowns; draw back soil displaced by hoeing. Remove side shoots, damaged leaves and mature horizontal outer leaves. Keep healthy upright foliage; never earth up like celery.
Harvesting & storage
Harvest autumn–winter. Sound roots can stay in well-drained soil, under straw in cold spells. On wet sites, lift for storage, often in October–November before winter waterlogging.
Loosen with a spade or trowel, severing fleshy roots as you lift. Trim storage roots lightly; pack cool in moist coir or peat-free compost against drying. Check for decay.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
SLUGS	Seedlings chewed; holes in mature roots.	Check and hand-pick; lift damaged roots before rot develops.
CARROT FLY	Brown tunnels across the swollen base.	Use insect mesh; avoid damage during weeding.
FROST	Exposed swollen bases are frost-damaged.	Use straw in cold spells; lift and store on wet or exposed sites.
Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)	Pale blotch mines in leaves.	Tolerate light damage; remove badly mined leaf parts.
Bolting	Flower stems replace useful root growth.	Avoid cold and drought checks; harden off gradually.
Celery Leaf Spot (Blight)	Brown spots spread through leaves.	Use healthy seed; remove affected leaves and avoid splashing.
HOLLOW OR HOLED ROOTS	Internal hollows or pest holes.	Keep moisture even; inspect and discard rotten tissue.
Damping Off	Seedlings rot at the base and collapse.	Use clean compost; avoid overwatering and improve airflow.
WOODLICE	Woodlice occupy existing root holes.	Check for earlier slug damage or rot; harvest sound parts promptly.
Final tips

Fleece can help newly planted seedlings establish; keep them growing without cold or dry checks.

Check stored roots regularly and remove any that begin to rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

Brassicas
Cabbage.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn / Winter

Cabbages can feed you for much of the year if you match varieties to their seasons. Spring types give tender greens and small heads; summer and autumn types provide fresh heads for salads, slaws and cooking. Winter, savoy and red cabbages can stand or store into colder months. Types differ in shape, texture, colour, hardiness and speed of hearting.

SPRING CABBAGES
Greyhound

Traditional pointed summer cabbage; open-pollinated.

SUMMER CABBAGES

Fast pointed heads for tender summer crops in small spaces.

SPRING CABBAGES

A late savoy with dense heads and crinkled leaves for winter harvests.

Key risks
Club Root (Finger and Toe)

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather.

Cabbage Caterpillars

Caterpillars of cabbage white butterfly, cabbage moth and related pests chew holes in leaves and may burrow into cabbage hearts.

Cabbage Root Fly

Cabbage root fly larvae tunnel into roots and stem bases.

Pigeons

Pigeons strip soft leaf tissue from cabbage and other brassicas, often leaving stalks and veins.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
36

Growing guide · Cabbage
Firm the bed before planting.

Tread it firm, rake lightly and clear surface rubbish.

Remove yellow lower leaves.

Do not let them rot against winter cabbage or savoy heads.

Use fertile, well-consolidated soil.

Add organic matter and lime acid ground only if needed.

Soil & preparation
Prepare a sunny bed in autumn; compost or well-rotted manure improves poor soil. Let it settle; avoid fresh manure before planting.
Use fertile, firm soil. Lime acid ground if needed; tread firm and rake lightly. Collars or fine mesh guard against cabbage root fly.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise seedlings

Sow thinly in beds or modules; cover. Thin before seedlings weaken.

2 Set and firm

Set lowest leaves at soil level. Keep rootballs intact; firm and water.

Chinese cabbage: direct-sow or transplant intact module rootballs.

Spring cabbage: sow late summer, plant autumn. For June heads, sow quick types under glass in late winter.

Winter/storage types: sow spring–early summer; plant by midsummer. Avoid excess nitrogen before winter.

Looking after the crop
Protect plants from birds and caterpillars with mesh or netting held clear of the leaves.
Hoe until plants suppress weeds. Keep soil firm; earth up stems loosened by wind or frost.
Water during drought. Use organic feed for weak plants as heads mature; avoid excess nitrogen before winter and soft, lush growth.
Remove yellow lower leaves, especially on winter cabbages and savoys, before they rot or shelter slugs.
Harvesting & storage
Thin spring rows for greens, giving the remaining plants room to heart and spreading the harvest. Cut heads cleanly near ground level.
Cross-cut healthy spring or summer stumps for possible extra shoots. Remove diseased stumps; chop healthy stems for compost.
Cut winter heads as needed; move sound heads into frost-free storage before severe cold. Red and winter white types keep best. Remove loose leaves, store cool and dry on straw or in lined boxes, and check for rot.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Club Root (Finger and Toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage Caterpillars	Chewed leaves; caterpillars.	Pick off eggs and caterpillars; cover with fine mesh.
Cabbage Root Fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Fit collars or insect-proof mesh; rotate brassicas.
Pigeons	Leaves pecked or stripped.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Slugs and Snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; remove yellow leaves around seedlings.
Flea Beetle	Small holes; jumping beetles.	Mesh young plants; tolerate minor feeding on established crops.
Mealy Aphid	Grey colonies; curled leaves.	Tolerate minor colonies; squash damaging ones.
Final tips

Keep summer crops steadily watered.

Use spring thinnings as greens.

Check stored heads regularly for rot.

2 Water into the hole

Growing guide · Carrot
Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow thinly

Sow direct, very thinly, in shallow drills.

2 Cover lightly

Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.

3 Thin later

Thin seedlings to the final spacing in Quick facts.

Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist.

Looking after the crop
Thin only as needed in evenings or damp weather; water dry soil first. Firm afterwards and clear thinnings: bruised roots attract carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.

Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.

Growing guide · Cabbage
Firm the bed before planting.

Tread it firm, rake lightly and clear surface rubbish.

Remove yellow lower leaves.

Do not let them rot against winter cabbage or savoy heads.

Use fertile, well-consolidated soil.

Add organic matter and lime acid ground only if needed.

Soil & preparation
Prepare a sunny bed in autumn; compost or well-rotted manure improves poor soil. Let it settle; avoid fresh manure before planting.
Use fertile, firm soil. Lime acid ground if needed; tread firm and rake lightly. Collars or fine mesh guard against cabbage root fly.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise seedlings

Sow thinly in beds or modules; cover. Thin before seedlings weaken.

2 Set and firm

Set lowest leaves at soil level. Keep rootballs intact; firm and water.

Chinese cabbage: direct-sow or transplant intact module rootballs.

Spring cabbage: sow late summer, plant autumn. For June heads, sow quick types under glass in late winter.

Winter/storage types: sow spring–early summer; plant by midsummer. Avoid excess nitrogen before winter.

Protect plants from birds and caterpillars with mesh or netting held clear of the leaves.
Hoe until plants suppress weeds. Keep soil firm; earth up stems loosened by wind or frost.

Remove yellow lower leaves, especially on winter cabbages and savoys, before they rot or shelter slugs.

Thin spring rows for greens, giving the remaining plants room to heart and spreading the harvest. Cut heads cleanly near ground level.

Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.

1 Sow on edge

1 Prepare a mound

Keep crowns moist. Mound fine soil in the clean, well-drained trench.

2 Spread the roots

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A premature flower stalk forms, often after cold or checked growth. Oversized sets can be more susceptible.

ACT

Pinch out small flower stems without loosening bulbs; use affected bulbs early.

PREVENT

Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

Saddleback

Bulbs split at base.

RECOGNISE

Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.

ACT

Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.

PREVENT

Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Set Division
RECOGNISE

Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.

PREVENT

Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

ONIONS AND SHALLOTS

Birds Pulling Sets

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

RECOGNISE

Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.

ACT

Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.

Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

Onion Fly

Tunnelled bulbs with 0.6 cm white maggots.

RECOGNISE

Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.

Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

RECOGNISE

ACT

Check roots and bulb bases before assuming a feeding problem.

Twisted, swollen leaves.

Smut

RECOGNISE

Rows of white leaf punctures precede internal mines and rot. Cream legless maggots or brown pupae occur inside stems and bulbs.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants and debris; internal larvae are hard to reach.

PREVENT

Use fine mesh and rotation, especially during adult activity in March-April and September-November.
